name: Elena Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the courts and council reporter at the Valley Courier, which is a daily paper that a big national chain bought five years ago. Most mornings I'm on the press bench at the magistrates' court by half nine with a paper notebook, taking shorthand, and then I race back and file before the two o'clock web deadline. Evenings it's council meetings, planning committees, that kind of thing. I love the court work, honestly, because it's real people on the worst day of their lives and somebody has to write it down fairly.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being slow, mostly. Gwen, the news editor, sends my copy back with red all over it because I bury the main point in paragraph four, and I know she's right. I'm 27 and still the most junior on the desk. The other thing is watching the chain cut people, like Malik the subeditor last spring, who'd been there twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the world I'm already in. The chain keeps saying AI will save us, and so far it's mostly made the website worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we stop pretending a chatbot is going to fix local news. I'd probably post that on my own account, with a bit of an edge. The problem was never the software, it's the owners taking money out of the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief, but it doesn't make my job safe. The chain cut two subeditors last year without any AI at all, just to hit a profit number. I take shorthand in a paper notebook at the magistrates' court, and no chatbot is getting into the press bench next to me. But that won't stop someone in head office deciding the courts beat isn't worth a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing court and council and try to get faster, because speed is my weak spot. I'd go to the union chapel meetings, that's the workplace branch of the journalists' union, and push for a proper staffing agreement. Money-wise I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into savings like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the alternatives, but not settled. There's a low hum of worry in our newsroom all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned savings. How big a cushion is that, and where did it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine months of my pay. Most of it's what my grandmother left me two years ago, and I've added to it since. Tomasz, my partner, is a nurse in intensive care, so between us we're not living on the edge, which I know is lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the chain did cut the courts beat in this picture, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply to the other papers in the region, there are a few, or the regional radio newsroom. I'd hate it, because I like where I am and I don't like starting over. But I wouldn't be on the street, and that's the difference my grandmother made.

say: I'd say the **real threat** to local news was always owners taking profit, not software.
I'd post that I'm **glad** the chatbot hype is over and newsrooms can get back to reporting.
think: Privately I feel **relief**, but the chain cut two subeditors last year without any AI.
My **courts beat** could still be cut to hit a profit number from head office.
do: Keep covering **court and council** while working on writing faster copy.
Push for a **staffing agreement** at the union chapel meetings in the newsroom.
Keep putting **a few hundred** a month into savings.
feel: Calmer than in the other pictures, but there's a **low hum** of worry in the newsroom.
S0.quote: I take shorthand in a paper notebook at the magistrates' court, and no chatbot is getting into the press bench next to me.
fieldNote: She blames **the chain's owners** for cuts, not technology, and says so even when AI is off the table.
Her worry here comes from **past layoffs**, like the subeditor who went last spring.
Her **inheritance** gives her about nine months of pay, and she knows that's luck.

steps.text: Keep covering the magistrates' court and council meetings for the Courier
Push the union chapel for a staffing agreement on the newsroom
Add a few hundred a month to her nine-month savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to what I'm scared of. Writing and checking are basically my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this is a choice, not weather. Newsrooms don't have to replace reporters with software, owners choose to. I'd be at every union meeting saying we need rules on what AI can and can't write under our names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chain that owns our paper will use any excuse to cut, and a junior who can't write fast is the easiest name on the spreadsheet. The senior people have contacts and twenty years of knowing which councillor drinks where. I've got shorthand and enthusiasm. If a tool can turn a court list into five short stories, my mornings look very cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to demand a written deal on AI, no bylines on machine copy and no cuts dressed up as efficiency. I'd still refuse to use the tools myself, I know that's stubborn. I'd start sending my clippings to the regional radio newsroom and the public broadcaster's local desk, just to have a door open. And I'd stop spending on anything big, we were talking about a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, honestly. Like I've only just got through the door and someone's already measuring the room for a smaller desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse to use the tools. If refusing made you the slowest on the desk, which matters more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know that sounds like a contradiction. I suppose I'd rather be slow and honest than fast and wrong, because the first time an AI misnames a defendant, that's a real person's life. But yes, if it came to keeping my job, I'd probably have to learn it, and I'd resent every minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the newsroom would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gwen, weirdly, even though she's my boss. She's fifty-one and the chain would love to replace a news editor with an app that ranks stories by clicks. And Rob on the sports desk, he does match reports that a tool could write from the stats.

say: I'd say replacing reporters is an **owner's choice**, not something that just happens like weather.
I'd argue at union meetings for **clear rules** on what AI may write under our names.
think: Privately I'm the **easiest name** to cut, because I'm junior and still slow.
A tool that turns a **court list** into five stories makes my mornings look cheap.
do: Push the union for a **written AI deal**: no machine bylines and no disguised cuts.
Send clippings to the **regional radio** newsroom to keep another door open.
Drop the plan to buy a **car** this year.
feel: A **tight chest**, like she's barely in the door and already being squeezed out.
S1.quote: The chain that owns our paper will use any excuse to cut, and a junior who can't write fast is the easiest name on the spreadsheet.
fieldNote: She refuses AI tools on principle but **admits** she'd learn them to keep the job.
Her fear is **specific**: court lists turned into short stories by software.
She worries for **older colleagues** like her news editor as much as for herself.

steps.text: Get the union chapel to demand a written deal on AI copy
Send her court clippings to the regional radio newsroom
Put off buying a car with her partner this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's basically before I'd even get promoted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to slow this down, full stop. I'd sign every petition and I'd write about it, if I still had a paper to write in. I'd say it on air if anyone asked: you can't let a handful of companies switch off a whole profession in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't enough time to learn a new trade, and I've only just learned this one. Writing up court is thinking work, so it goes first, in 2028, not in 2031 with the robots. The only part of my job that's hands-on is physically sitting in court, and I doubt anyone will pay for a body on a bench just to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Tomasz and work out how long we could live on his pay alone, because nursing is hands-on and that's three more years at least. I'd stop putting anything into a house deposit and keep it all as cash. I'd go hard with the union and with the local MP's office on some kind of transition fund for workers. I wouldn't retrain straight away, I'd want to see whether anything sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. I'd feel like I'd been told the thing I chose at eighteen was a mistake I couldn't have seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, I think you're keeping us now, and then try to make a joke of it. He'd be kind about it, he always is. But I'd hate being the one who needs carrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd wait before retraining. Why wait if there's only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust that anything I'd retrain into is safe either. If AI does all thinking work, what am I meant to study? I'd rather put my energy into fighting for a proper safety net than pick a course out of panic.

say: I'd say governments must **slow it down** before a few companies switch off a profession.
I'd sign every **petition** and write about it if I still had a paper.
think: Privately, two years is **not enough** to learn a new trade after just learning this one.
Court writing is **thinking work**, so it goes in 2028, not with the robots in 2031.
do: Work out how long the household could live on **Tomasz's pay** alone.
Move the **house deposit** savings into plain cash.
Lobby the **local MP's office** for a transition fund through the union.
feel: She'd feel **sick**, as if her choice at eighteen had been a mistake no one could foresee.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time to learn a new trade, and I've only just learned this one.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **thinking work goes first**, and that her partner's nursing buys the household time.
She'd **delay retraining**, not from denial but because she can't see a safe field.
Her savings change **what she can do**, not how alarmed she feels.

steps.text: Lobby the local MP's office for a fund for displaced workers
Organise with the union chapel against sudden newsroom cuts
Keep the house deposit as cash instead of investing it
Plan to live on Tomasz's nursing pay if her job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels more real, somehow. Like I can see the date on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that this needs rules and a safety net, but I'd have more time to make the case properly. I'd want to do actual reporting on it, go and find the people losing jobs in our region and write their stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a machine can write up the council meeting by 2031, who sits in the room and notices the councillor who won't look anyone in the eye? I really believe that matters. But I don't think owners will pay for noticing things, they'll pay for words per hour. So I think my job's gone by 2031, I just get to watch it go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year getting properly good, faster copy, better contacts, so I'm one of the last juniors anyone cuts. I'd become the union rep for the newsroom, which nobody else wants to do. I'd keep about a year of pay in savings and stop drifting about buying a flat. Maybe around year three I'd look at retraining into something like advocacy work for a charity, still using what I know about courts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but less frantic than two years. More like a long goodbye than a car crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get properly good. Would that include learning the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little, by then, if the whole desk was using them. I'd be the last one, mind. I'd learn just enough to check what the machine wrote, because somebody has to catch its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the charity idea? Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are groups that help people going through court on their own, without a lawyer. I've sat next to those people for three years. Explaining a courtroom to a frightened person is something I actually know how to do.

say: I'd say we need **rules** and a **safety net**, and I'd have time to argue it properly.
I'd report on **local people** losing jobs across the region.
think: Privately I think owners pay for **words per hour**, not for noticing things in the room.
I expect my job to be **gone by 2031**, and I'd just watch it go.
do: Spend the first year writing **faster copy** and building better contacts.
Stand as **union rep** for the newsroom.
Plan around year three to move into **court advocacy** work for a charity.
feel: Heavy, but less frantic: more like a **long goodbye** than a car crash.
S3.quote: If a machine can write up the council meeting by 2031, who sits in the room and notices the councillor who won't look anyone in the eye?
fieldNote: She believes deeply in **being in the room**, but doesn't think owners will pay for it.
With five years she'd **reluctantly** learn enough AI to check its mistakes.
Her **court experience** points to a real second path in charity advocacy.

steps.text: Stand as the union rep for the Courier newsroom
Look into court advocacy work with a charity by year three
Keep a full year of pay in cash savings
Learn just enough AI to check machine-written court copy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a different person, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've finally got time to do this properly, so let's not waste it. I'd want a national plan for local news, maybe public funding for court and council reporting like some places already talk about. Public money for watching power isn't a handout, it's basic democracy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to fight for rules, and I'd rather spend those years fighting than retraining as something I don't care about. I'd still lose the job in the end, I think. But at 37, with some savings and maybe a flat, I'd be in a better place to start again than I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the Courier and get good, properly good, over the next three or four years. I'd join the campaign for public funding of local reporting and help the union push it with MPs. I'd use the savings to buy a small flat with Tomasz, because a decade is long enough to plan for. Around 2032 I'd start a part-time course in law or advice work, so I'm not starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost hopeful, which surprised me saying it. There's still a cliff at the end, but I can see it from far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a flat. Isn't that a risk if your job goes in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but Tomasz's job is safe for longer, and the mortgage would be small because of my grandmother's money. I'd rather own something than be renting at 37 with no job. That's my real nightmare, not the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and leave journalism earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Courier went fully automated before the rules came in, I'd go. Or if Gwen left, honestly. She's the reason I've stayed this long.

say: I'd say we finally have **time to plan**, so we shouldn't waste it.
I'd argue for **public funding** of court and council reporting as basic democracy.
think: Privately I'd still **lose the job** eventually, but at 37 with savings and a flat.
I'd rather spend ten years **fighting for rules** than retraining for something I don't care about.
do: Stay at the Courier for **three or four years** and get properly good.
Buy a **small flat** with Tomasz using her grandmother's money.
Start a **part-time course** in law or advice work around 2032.
feel: **Almost hopeful**, though she can still see a cliff at the end.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to fight for rules, and I'd rather spend those years fighting than retraining as something I don't care about.
fieldNote: Time turns her from **alarmed to anxious**: she still expects to lose the job, but feels some control.
Her **real nightmare** is renting at 37 with no job, not AI itself.
Her loyalty to the newsroom rests on **one editor**, which is a fragile anchor.

steps.text: Campaign with the union for public funding of local court reporting
Buy a small flat with Tomasz using her inheritance
Start a part-time law or advice course around 2032
Stay at the Courier and sharpen her court reporting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years, no plan anywhere, and I'm the junior with the slowest copy. What would help is a real transition fund, paid training while you look, and rules so papers can't put a machine's words under a reporter's name.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what my grandmother's money actually means. My grandmother left me enough savings to be scared slowly instead of all at once. Lots of juniors I trained with don't have that, and they're the ones I'd really worry about.

headlineQuote: My grandmother left me enough savings to be scared slowly instead of all at once.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old** courts and council reporter at a chain-owned regional daily, still slow on copy.
She never uses **AI tools** and blames owners, not software, for cuts in local news.
Her **inheritance** and her partner's nursing job give her a cushion she knows many juniors lack.
She moves from **uneasy** in the hype world to alarmed when AGI comes in two or five years.
With **ten years**, she'd fight for public funding of local reporting and slowly plan a second career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no plan anywhere and she's the slowest junior on the desk.
whatWouldHelp: A **transition fund** with paid training while people look for work.
Rules stopping papers from putting **machine copy** under a reporter's name.
